title: 🍂 Prime before the fall
body_text: The announcements for the winners of this year’s Nobel Prize awards got underway yesterday, as US psychiatrist Karl Deisseroth and two German colleagues received this year’s prize in Physiology or Medicine for their research on the inner workings of the human brain. The three scientists, who will share the ~$1.2 million prize money, can only hope that their work stands the test of time a little longer than the recipient of the same award 100 years ago. Danish pathologist Johannes Fibiger picked up the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1926 for his work identifying a parasitic worm as a cause of stomach cancer in rats, but his research was proved wrong only a few years later , and the award has gone down as one of the rare cases of a mistakenly awarded Nobel Prize. Seemingly unperturbed by the fact that no one has ever referred to its latter-year promotional period by its official (and overlong) title, Amazon is pushing its “Prime Big Deal Days” again, with ads and somehow-not-sponsored editorials for various offers inevitably cluttering news feeds and inboxes today and tomorrow. This two-day discount window is the younger and smaller sibling of Amazon’s original summertime Prime Day, having first been introduced four years ago and lasting for just 48 hours, compared to the four-day stretch of the June 2026 event. The promotions are big business for Amazon, as investors who keep a keen eye on the company’s quarterly reports will be aware, after it shifted the summer event to see the sales uptick in Q2 rather than Q3 this year . Luckily for Amazon, it seems that the secondary event is gathering a little more steam this year in comparison to previous editions. While summer searches for the main event have dwindled a little in the years since their peak eight years ago, US interest in the October Prime Day has reached a new high this year, according to partially complete data from Google . Despite ongoing questions around whether Amazon’s promotional events actually offer customers value for money, the figures suggest that shoppers are still eager to find out for themselves. Even as parts of Amazon’s business that aren’t selling-you-things-online-for-cheap — such as its burgeoning AI and custom chip businesses — continue to grow , online retail sales still account for the lion’s share of its top-line revenue figures, making shifting products at lower prices around Prime Days a bit of a no-brainer for the company. Bezos’ company also has more paying users to target with discounts and deals than ever before. When the company hosted its first Prime Day in July 2015 to celebrate its 20th anniversary, just 54 million US shoppers used Prime; last year, that figure had ballooned to a staggering 201 million. That’s how much “Digger,” the Tom Cruise-led satire that marks Warner Bros’ last release before its $111 billion merger with Paramount is expected to close today, made across North American theaters in its opening weekend. The disappointing haul (down, even, from the $12 million to $15 million that Warner execs had pessimistically penciled in) is Cruise’s lowest domestic debut since “Lions for Lambs” in 2007, per The Hollywood Reporter . With a reported budget of around $160 million, the underwhelming first weekend box office figure could set “Digger” up as one of the biggest commercial flops in recent history. In sad news for Cruise heads around the world, it’s also looking like yet another setback on the megastar’s decades-long quest to get his hands on a competitive Oscar, with his latest departure from the action roles he’s become known for currently sitting at a lowly 51% critics’ rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes . Chips and dip: Intel dropped yesterday after Elon Musk confirmed talks between TSMC and his Terafab chip venture around potential collaboration. EV sales in the EU hit a new record for January to August this year, according to a study from a Brussels environmental advocacy agency, with new research showing that deliveries may rose 45% from 2025 to 1.64 million. OpenAI announced that it will test new visual ad format to ChatGPT, which it noted reaches 1.2 billion people per week, debuting the new style with people generating images on the platform. Meta and Microsoft are working to get their own employees to use Anthropic’s Claude less, The Information reports . The US currently reigns supreme, counting 432 prizes, compared to the UK which sits in a distant second place with a tally of 148, per World Population Review . title: 👟 Nike’s plan to make Jordans cool again
body_text: One lawyer learned the hard way that ChatGPT is not a witness. New Mexico attorney Stephen Aarons used ChatGPT to help write a brief for a murder appeal — only for it to invent witnesses and testimony that never existed. “It’s little comfort to know that my stupidity is what brings us together this afternoon,” Aarons told five judges . The court fined him $5,000 and kicked him off the case. Stocks finished up on Friday, pushing the week into positive territory. It’s been a rough few years for Nike , and so far its comeback plans haven’t managed to get sales growing again. Its next act: rethinking Jordan. The brand accounted for 13% of Nike’s global business last quarter, but revenue fell by the mid-teens. On a call with analysts on Thursday, CEO Elliott Hill offered a pretty straightforward diagnosis: “Simply put, we've been oversupplying our iconic retro product, asking them to do too much.” The company will reduce the volume and frequency of specific Jordan retro launches. If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is: Nike faced a similar problem with Jordan nearly a decade ago, after ramping up production left too many sneakers sitting on shelves. Its solution then was the same as it is now: make fewer shoes and create a “pull market” where consumers chase rare shoes. “When consumers see the Jumpman, it should feel special,” Hill said. “It should feel earned. And every decision we're making is designed to ensure the Jordan Brand remains as coveted a decade from now as it has been for the past several decades” The revamp comes as the company reported quarterly financials that disappointed investors. On Thursday, Nike reported: Quarterly earnings per share at $0.48, more than the $0.43 analysts were expecting. But also reported $11.2 billion in sales for the quarter, less than the 11.3 billion expected, and about a 4% decline year over year. Nike said it expects sales to decline by “high-single digits” in the fiscal year. The company’s biggest sales decline is in China, where revenue plunged 26% year over year. The company’s gloomy guidance “assumes that China actually gets worse from a revenue perspective for the balance of this year,” CFO Dave Denton told analysts. “Correcting these issues will take time and an inflection back to sales growth is now not likely until calendar 2028, at the earliest,” analysts at Telsey Group wrote in a Friday note. Over the past few years, Nike has battled with a medley of issues: tariffs on imported goods, a “cautious” consumer, and increasing competition from footwear upstarts like Hoka and On, as well as old competitors like New Balance and Adidas . title: 💣 Creative destruction prepares to go public
body_text: Dutch company Robin Radar was formed five decades ago to produce unique radar systems designed to detect birds, mostly to ensure that planes landing at major airports can avoid dangerous flocks. This was a solid and reliable business for a while, a charming little niche of detecting speedy, small airborne organisms that can cause large problems for expensive infrastructure and endanger human life. Then, of course, came drones, and then the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and then the shifting reality of warfare towards cheap, flimsy drones loaded up with explosives. Yet again, a new form of the core problem solved by Robin Radar — detecting speedy, small airborne robots that can cause large problems for expensive infrastructure and endanger human life — emerged, and needless to say business has really taken off . Bloomberg reports that Anthropic, which had been known to be eyeing an IPO sometime after November’s mid-term elections, is aiming to go public before Thanksgiving . Earlier this week, Reuters scored a copy of the Anthropic prospectus , and traders have spent the last several days digesting it. To say that the numbers in the report are jaw-dropping and eye-popping is an insult to mandibular and ocular versatility. On one hand, the good numbers: Revenue 12x’d in 2025, hitting $4.6 billion, though they lost $8 billion on an operating basis. They spent $7.33 billion on compute alone, which was more than half of the $12.65 billion in operating expenses. Big numbers, but not exactly shocking. On the other, the bad ones: “On an operating basis” excludes writedowns of liabilities related to previous fundraising; the company reported a net loss of $42 billion in 2025. Still, those numbers are still downright small, compared to… The crazy one? Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on cloud. A half-trillion on cloud. That’s the kind of number that gets people thinking this better be worth it. Then, of course, the only one that really matters: how much this company's gonna be worth. For that, SpaceX is the bar to beat, and reportedly Anthropic is eyeing $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion. Earlier this year, SpaceX's IPO managed to underscore just how little revenue investors really needed to see to grant a multi-trillion dollar valuation. One reason for the interest at any price? So far, the only way that investors in public markets have managed to invest in AI laboratories has been indirectly. Either they've bought the companies that supply these labs — the chip manufacturers, the data center operators — as an implicit bet on the ultimate demand for this tech. The other alternative is investing in the hyperscalers — Alphabet and Meta — who have an AI lab as a subsidiary, the downside being that the actual AI laboratory's impact on their share prices is a mere drop in the bucket compared to the vast amounts of valuation derived from their mature advertising business. The last way to get in on the trade as an investor in public markets would, presumably, be to bet against the long-term performance of the companies that will be disrupted by the tech. When one public company does something that takes market share from another public company, investors are able to react by buying the former and selling the latter, in the aggregate increasing the valuation of the former and reducing the valuation of the latter. But when a non-public AI lab revealed that they were able to compete with the core offerings of a public company, things are less direct: recall the hits taken by the trucking business, the cybersecurity business , the SaaS business , and the consulting business whenever a white paper implied that OpenAI or Anthropic was poised to eat their lunch. This led to the interesting paradox where, essentially, private Anthropic would release tech demonstration that would destroy a lot of the value of a cohort of public companies, but there was no direct commensurate creation of value elsewhere in the stock market. This is irritating for investors, potentially irritating enough for them to overlook the eye-watering value-to-revenue ratio on display here.
